title: Syntax Error
genre: 1979 new wave of British heavy metal
description: Syntax Error is the 1979 fourth album from Procedural Byts: twelve tracks of new wave of British heavy metal about programming languages themselves. Nyble sings lead and plays bass, Byt plays lead guitar, and Bytes plays drums and sings backup. Side A covers how code is read and run: lexers, parsers, compilers and interpreters, types, scope and garbage collection. Side B is functional programming, and it has no guitar, because Byt refused to play songs with no side effects. Lambdas, pure functions, immutability, map, filter, reduce and closures, all driven by fuzz bass and drums. Byt comes back for the closer, Paradigm Shift. Play loud. Parse carefully.
tagline: The 1979 NWOBHM album from Procedural Byts: a programming languages course in twelve songs, with a whole side of no guitar.
lineup: Still a power trio, mostly. Nyble sings lead on every song and plays bass guitar. Byt plays lead guitar on Side A and the closer. Bytes plays drums and sings backup. Side B is just Nyble and Bytes.

members.name: Nyble
members.bio: Four bits and, on Side B, the entire string section. Nyble sings lead on every song and took over every riff and solo on the functional side, through a fuzz pedal she has never turned off since.

members.name: Byt
members.bio: One bit, with strong opinions about side effects. Byt plays lead guitar and most of the solos on Side A, sits out Side B on principle, and comes back for the closer louder than ever.

members.name: Bytes
members.bio: Eight bits and, with no guitar to hide behind, suddenly very audible. Bytes plays drums and sings backup, and on Side B he took the solos on No Side Effects and Map, Filter, Reduce.

members.name: Null
members.bio: Sat out Side B with Byt. Has not said whether it agreed with him.

story.heading: Side B Has No Guitar
paragraphs: In 1979 the band set out to make an album about programming languages themselves: how code gets read, checked, translated and run, and the different ways of thinking that languages give you.
Side A went smoothly. Lexers, parsers, compilers, types and scope, and a garbage collector Bytes described as “the roadie we always needed.”

Side B was going to be functional programming. Byt read the lyric sheet for No Side Effects, put his guitar back in its case, and announced that he would not play on any song that didn’t change the world. Nyble pointed out that functional programs do change the world, just at the edges. Byt said the edges were exactly where he would be standing.

So Side B has no guitar. Nyble played lead on bass through a fuzz pedal, and Bytes played the drums like they owed him money. Reviewers called it a bold minimalist turn. Byt called it a principled stand. Null sat next to him on the studio steps the whole time, in solidarity or by coincidence.
Byt came back for the final track, Paradigm Shift, on the grounds that a paradigm shift is the biggest side effect there is. Nobody argued.

The title came from the first test pressing, which skipped so badly the factory stamped SYNTAX ERROR on the sleeve as a warning. The band liked it better than their own title, which nobody can remember.

cover_sub: The fourth album, 1979. Side A is how code is read and run. Side B is functional, and has no guitar.

songs.title: Lexer of the Damned

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: Characters stream in a river of text,
Letters and symbols, what comes next?
The lexer reads them and chops them in pieces,
Keywords, names and the numbers it releases!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Lexer of the damned! (Tokens!)
Breaking down the words of man! (Tokens!)
If and while and equals and the number nine,
Lexer of the damned, read it line by line!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: Throw away the spaces, throw away the notes,
Comments are for humans, the compiler never quotes.
X equals five is a name, a sign, a number in a row,
Three little tokens, and on to the parser they go!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Keyword! (If!) Identifier! (X!)
Operator! (Plus!) Literal! (Six!)

parts.label: Lead guitar solo: Byt
parts.desc: Byt plays one long continuous run, then chops it into short separate pieces with silence between each, the way a lexer turns a stream of characters into tokens.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Lexer of the damned! (Tokens!)
Breaking down the words of man! (Tokens!)
If and while and equals and the number nine,
Lexer of the damned, read it line by line!

songs.note: Side A. The opening riff is the album’s source code, read one token at a time.
songs.lesson: The first step in compiling is lexical analysis. The lexer, or scanner, reads source text and groups characters into tokens like keywords, identifiers, operators and literals, throwing away whitespace and comments. The tokens then go to the parser.

songs.title: Parse Tree

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: The tokens come in order but they don’t know what they mean,
The parser has the grammar and it builds the tree unseen.
A statement made of expressions, expressions made of terms,
The root up at the top, and the leaves down with the worms!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Parse tree! Branches of the law!
Parse tree! Grammar without flaw!
Times before the plus, it’s written in the rules,
Parse tree, parse tree, and the grammar never fools!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: But miss a single bracket and the tree will never grow,
The parser stops and screams at you, it wants you all to know.
Syntax error! Line fourteen! Expected a semicolon!
The tree lies broken on the ground, a promise that was stolen!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Syntax! (The shape is right!)
Semantics! (The meaning’s right!)
A sentence can be perfect and still be wrong tonight!

parts.label: Lead guitar solo: Byt
parts.desc: Byt starts with one phrase, the root, which splits into two answering phrases, then four, then eight, building a tree out of melody. One wrong note and the band stops cold: syntax error.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Parse tree! Branches of the law!
Parse tree! Grammar without flaw!
Times before the plus, it’s written in the rules,
Parse tree, parse tree, and the grammar never fools!

songs.note: Side A. The most structured song on the album, by definition.
songs.lesson: A parser checks tokens against a grammar (often written in BNF) and builds a parse tree or abstract syntax tree. The grammar encodes structure like operator precedence. A syntax error means the code doesn’t fit the grammar. Syntax is form and semantics is meaning: code can parse perfectly and still be wrong.

songs.title: Compile or Interpret

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: The compiler takes your program and it reads it through and through,
It turns it all to machine code before it runs for you.
It catches errors early and it runs it fast and clean,
But change a single line and you rebuild the whole machine!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Compile it! (All at once!)
Interpret it! (Line by line!)
One translates before it runs, the other in real time,
Compile or interpret, choose your poison, choose your line!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: The interpreter reads a line and does it right away,
No waiting for the build, you change your mind and play.
And in between, the bytecode for a virtual machine,
Write it once and run it anywhere the VM’s ever been!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Compile time! (Caught before it runs!)
Run time! (Caught when it’s begun!)

parts.label: Lead guitar solo: Byt
parts.desc: Byt plays the solo twice. The first time, every note is worked out in advance and played at full speed: compiled. The second time, he makes it up note by note as he goes: interpreted.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Compile it! (All at once!)
Interpret it! (Line by line!)
One translates before it runs, the other in real time,
Compile or interpret, choose your poison, choose your line!

songs.note: Side A. Byt plays the solo twice, two different ways. Most people can’t tell which one is which.
songs.lesson: A compiler translates a whole program into machine code before it runs, so it executes fast and catches many errors early. An interpreter runs code directly, statement by statement, so it’s quicker to change but slower to run. Many languages take the middle path: compile to bytecode and run it on a virtual machine.

songs.title: Strongly Typed

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: I won’t add a word to a number, I won’t mix the steel and stone,
Every value has a type, and every type stands on its own.
Don’t cast me where I don’t belong, don’t bend me out of shape,
Add a string to a number and there’s no escape!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Strongly typed! (Static!)
Checked before you run!
Strongly typed! (Dynamic!)
Checked when it’s begun!
Know your types, know your types, the errors fall away,
Strongly typed, and the bugs don’t live to see the day!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: Static types are checked when you compile, before it ever starts,
Dynamic types are checked while running, tagged on all the parts.
A weak type bends and guesses, turns a word into a five,
And inference finds the type for you, it keeps the code alive!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Type error! (Type error!) An integer’s not a String!
Type error! (Type error!) You can’t do that kind of thing!

parts.label: Bass solo: Nyble
parts.desc: Byt tries to steer the song into a different key four times, and Nyble’s bass refuses every time, dragging it back. You can’t put a value of one type where another belongs.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Strongly typed! (Static!)
Checked before you run!
Strongly typed! (Dynamic!)
Checked when it’s begun!
Know your types, know your types, the errors fall away,
Strongly typed, and the bugs don’t live to see the day!

songs.note: Side A. Nyble’s answer to every argument the band had in 1979.
songs.lesson: A type system classifies values and stops invalid operations. Static typing checks types at compile time (as in Java and C); dynamic typing checks them while the program runs (as in Python). Strong typing refuses to mix types silently, while weak typing quietly converts them. Type inference lets the compiler work out types you didn’t write.

songs.title: Lexical Scope

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: A name is born inside a block, it lives inside its walls,
Outside the curly braces, no one answers when it calls.
Look inside the nearest block, then the one outside,
Out and out until the global, where the last names hide!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Lexical scope! (Where were you born?)
Lexical scope! (Where were you sworn?)
Read the code and you can see which name is which,
Lexical scope, and the meaning doesn’t switch!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: Name a local like a global and you’ll shadow it from view,
The inner one hides the outer one, the outer can’t get through.
Dynamic scope would ask who called you, wherever that may be,
But lexical just reads the page, and that’s the way to see!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Binding! (Name to value!)
Shadowing! (Hidden from view!)

parts.label: Lead guitar solo: Byt
parts.desc: Byt plays a phrase inside a phrase inside a phrase. The innermost one repeats a note from the outer ones and for a moment hides them completely: shadowing. Then the outer melody comes back into view.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Lexical scope! (Where were you born?)
Lexical scope! (Where were you sworn?)
Read the code and you can see which name is which,
Lexical scope, and the meaning doesn’t switch!

songs.note: Side A. The vocals were recorded in three rooms, one inside the other.
songs.lesson: Scope is where a name can be seen. With lexical (static) scope, which most languages use, a name refers to the nearest enclosing declaration in the source text, searching outward to the global level. An inner declaration with the same name shadows the outer one. Dynamic scope looks names up through the chain of calls instead.

songs.title: Garbage Collector

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: New object, new object, filling up the heap,
Every time you make one there’s another one to keep.
But some of them are orphans and nobody holds their hand,
No reference points to them, they’re garbage on the land!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Garbage collector! Coming in the night!
Garbage collector! Clear the heap tonight!
Start at the roots and mark what you can reach,
Sweep away the rest, that’s the sermon that I preach!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: In C you free it by hand, every byte you take,
Forget and it’s a leak, free it twice and it’s a break!
The collector does it for you, but it takes a little time,
A pause to sweep the heap, a small price for the crime!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Mark! (Reachable!) Sweep! (Unreachable!)
Count the references! (Zero and it’s gone!)

parts.label: Lead guitar solo: Byt
parts.desc: Byt fills the solo with more and more notes until there’s barely room. Then he stops, keeps only the handful still connected to the main melody, and sweeps the rest away into silence.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Garbage collector! Coming in the night!
Garbage collector! Clear the heap tonight!
Start at the roots and mark what you can reach,
Sweep away the rest, that’s the sermon that I preach!

songs.note: Side A. The last song on Side A, and the last guitar Byt plays until the final track.
songs.lesson: Objects live on the heap. In languages like C, programmers free memory by hand, risking leaks and double frees. A garbage collector frees unreachable objects automatically: mark-and-sweep marks everything reachable from the roots and sweeps away the rest, while reference counting frees an object when nothing refers to it. Collection costs some pause time in exchange for safety.

songs.title: Lambda

parts.label: Intro (spoken)
lines: This is Side B. There is no guitar on Side B.
Byt says these songs have no side effects,
And he won’t play anything that doesn’t change the world.

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: A function with no name, a lambda in the dark,
Pass it like a value and let it make its mark.
Store it in a variable, hand it to a friend,
Functions are just data, from beginning to the end!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Lambda! (No name!)
Lambda! (Same game!)
Functions in and functions out, first-class all the way,
Lambda, lambda, functions are the values that we play!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: Take x, give back x times x, and never say its name,
Hand it to another function and it plays the game.
A function that returns a function, a function that takes two,
Higher and higher order, there’s nothing they can’t do!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Church had the calculus! (Lambda!)
Lisp had the parentheses! (Lambda!)

parts.label: Bass solo: Nyble
parts.desc: With no guitar, Nyble’s bass takes the lead: a short motif with no name that she hands to Bytes, who plays it on the toms and hands it back changed. A function passed around like a value.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Lambda! (No name!)
Lambda! (Same game!)
Functions in and functions out, first-class all the way,
Lambda, lambda, functions are the values that we play!

songs.note: Side B, no guitar. The first song on Side B. Byt sat this one out, and the next four.
songs.lesson: Functional programming treats functions as first-class values: they can be stored in variables, passed as arguments and returned from other functions. A lambda is an anonymous function, like `x -> x * x`. Functions that take or return functions are called higher-order. Lambda calculus, from Alonzo Church, is the theory underneath.

songs.title: No Side Effects

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: Same input, same output, every single time,
No hidden state, no secrets, no changing down the line.
I don’t print and I don’t save, I don’t touch the world outside,
A pure function, nothing more, with nothing left to hide!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: No side effects! (Nothing changes!)
No side effects! (Nothing rearranges!)
Call me twice and I’ll say the same thing back,
No side effects, and you can trust me on that!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: Replace the call with its answer and nothing in the world will change,
That’s referential transparency, and it isn’t even strange.
Easy to test and easy to prove and easy to run side by side,
The functions with no side effects have nothing left to hide!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: But you can’t print without an effect! (We know!)
Push them to the edges and let the middle flow!

parts.label: Drum solo: Bytes
parts.desc: Bytes plays the same eight-bar pattern four times, identical every time. Same input, same output. The crowd keeps waiting for him to change it. He never does.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: No side effects! (Nothing changes!)
No side effects! (Nothing rearranges!)
Call me twice and I’ll say the same thing back,
No side effects, and you can trust me on that!

songs.note: Side B, no guitar. The song Byt refused to play on. The title is why.
songs.lesson: A pure function’s result depends only on its inputs, and it causes no side effects: no printing, no changing variables, no input or output. You can replace any call with its result (referential transparency), which makes code easier to test, reason about and run in parallel. Real programs still need effects, so functional style pushes them to the edges.

songs.title: Immutable

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: Once a value’s made it stays, it never bends or breaks,
You can’t change it after, no matter what it takes.
Want a new list with one more? You make a brand-new one,
The old one stays forever as it was when it was done!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Immutable! (Carved in stone!)
Immutable! (Leave it alone!)
Nobody can change it behind your back,
Immutable, immutable, and there’s no going back!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: Two threads share a value and they never have to fight,
Nobody can change it, so there’s no one wrong or right.
Share the parts that didn’t change and copy just the new,
The old one and the new one, both of them are true!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Mutation! (Danger!) A change you didn’t see!
Immutable! (Safety!) The way it’s meant to be!

parts.label: Bass solo: Nyble
parts.desc: Nyble plays one riff and never changes it. Every new idea in the solo is played alongside the original, never on top of it, and the old riff is still there, untouched, at the end.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Immutable! (Carved in stone!)
Immutable! (Leave it alone!)
Nobody can change it behind your back,
Immutable, immutable, and there’s no going back!

songs.note: Side B, no guitar. Nyble’s bass part was recorded once and never touched again. Everything else was built around it.
songs.lesson: Immutable data can’t change after it’s created. “Updating” it makes a new value, often sharing the parts that didn’t change. That removes a whole class of bugs from surprise changes and makes it safe to share data between threads. Strings in Java are an everyday example.

songs.title: Map, Filter, Reduce

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: Take a list and a function, apply it to every one,
Map it down the line until the line is done.
Double every number, capitalize every name,
Same length on the other side, but nothing’s quite the same!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Map! (Change them all!)
Filter! (Let some fall!)
Reduce! (Into one!)
And the loop is done!
Map, filter, reduce, with no loop in sight,
Functions on the list, and the list comes out right!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: Filter takes a test and keeps the ones that pass,
Throw away the odd ones and keep the even class.
Reduce takes the list and folds it into one,
Add them all together and the counting’s done!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: No index! (No counter!) No i plus plus!
Say what you want, not how, and leave the how to us!

parts.label: Drum solo: Bytes
parts.desc: Bytes plays a pattern across every drum, then plays it again with each hit doubled: map. Then he drops every other hit: filter. Then he folds the whole thing into one enormous final hit: reduce.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Map! (Change them all!)
Filter! (Let some fall!)
Reduce! (Into one!)
And the loop is done!
Map, filter, reduce, with no loop in sight,
Functions on the list, and the list comes out right!

songs.note: Side B, no guitar. Bytes calls this the drum album. On this song, he is not wrong.
songs.lesson: Higher-order list operations replace explicit loops. Map applies a function to every element, filter keeps the elements that pass a test, and reduce (or fold) combines all the elements into one value. They describe what to compute rather than how, and they chain together naturally.

songs.title: Closure

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: A function made inside a function, born inside a room,
It remembers every variable that lived there in the gloom.
The outer one returns, and all its locals should be gone,
But the closure keeps them with it and it carries them along!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Closure! (Remember me!)
Closure! (Set it free!)
A function and the world it came from, wrapped up into one,
Closure, closure, it remembers when it’s done!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: Make a counter function and return the inner one,
It keeps the count inside it, hidden from everyone.
Call it once, it says one, call it twice, it says two,
The count lives in the closure, and it’s only seen by you!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Captured! (The variables!)
Enclosed! (The environment!)

parts.label: Bass solo: Nyble
parts.desc: Nyble’s solo starts inside the verse’s groove. Then the groove ends and the solo keeps going on its own, still carrying one note from the verse that nobody is playing anymore: the variable it captured.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Closure! (Remember me!)
Closure! (Set it free!)
A function and the world it came from, wrapped up into one,
Closure, closure, it remembers when it’s done!

songs.note: Side B, no guitar. The quietest song the band has ever recorded. It still isn’t quiet.
songs.lesson: A closure is a function bundled with the variables from the scope where it was created. It can keep using them after that scope has ended, as in a counter function that returns an inner function keeping its own private count. Closures make callbacks and private state possible.

songs.title: Paradigm Shift

parts.label: Intro (spoken)
lines: Ladies and gentlemen… the guitar.

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: Procedural, step by step, the recipe in a row,
Objects with their state and methods, everything they know.
Functional, the math of it, the pure and the clean,
Logic says just state the facts and the answer will be seen!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Paradigm shift! (Change the way you think!)
Paradigm shift! (Standing at the brink!)
Every language is a lens, and every lens a different view,
Paradigm shift, pick the one that’s right for you!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: Event-driven waits for clicks and answers when they call,
Most languages today, they borrow from them all.
Learn a second language and the first one makes more sense,
Every new paradigm will tear down another fence!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Imperative! (How!) Declarative! (What!)
Every paradigm’s a tool that you’ve got!

parts.label: Lead guitar solo: Byt
parts.desc: The guitar comes back. Byt plays a solo in four sections, each in a different style: step by step, built from small reusable pieces, pure repeating patterns, and finally one that only states where it wants to end up and lets the band get it there.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Paradigm shift! (Change the way you think!)
Paradigm shift! (Standing at the brink!)
Every language is a lens, and every lens a different view,
Paradigm shift, pick the one that’s right for you!

songs.note: Side B, guitar returns. Byt came back for the closer, on the grounds that a paradigm shift is the biggest side effect there is.
songs.lesson: Programming paradigms are different ways of thinking: imperative or procedural (steps that change state), object-oriented (objects with state and behavior), functional (pure functions and immutable data), logic (state facts and rules, as in Prolog) and event-driven (respond to events). Imperative code says how; declarative code says what. Most modern languages mix several.
